full_judgment:
5. The learned Sessions Judge, Khulna, after hearing the parties and upon considering the evidence and materials on record found the present appellants and other 8(eight) accused persons guilty under section 302/34 of the Penal Code in Sessions Case No.287 of 2000 arising out of Sonaganaga Police Station Case No. 09 dated 7.9.1999 corresponding to GR Case No. 1132 of 1999 and convicted them under the aforesaid sections and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life and also to pay a fine of Tk. 10,000/-each, in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1(one) more year by his judgment and order dated 22.02.2006. 

 8. Mr. Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that mere recovery of blood stained earth (mud) and fired cartridge may provide corroboration of the occurrence of causing death to the deceased by fire arm at the place of occurrence but it does not mean that the appellants committed the offence and the death of the deceased was caused by fire arm used by the appellants in the absence of any independent and direct evidence against the appellants. The learned advocate further submits that the High court Division relied upon the statement of P Ws.3 and 4 who also made statements under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and thereby affirmed the judgment of the trial Court in respect of the appellants which is ex- facie illegal and not sustainable in the eye of law. Because without any direct and/or legal evidence conviction and sentences cannot be sustained on the basis of statements of witnesses under section 164 of the Code. Moreover, both these two witnesses were declared hostile while they deposed as PWs. 3 and 4 and the evidence of a hostile witness is not acceptable if not corroborated by other witnesses in material particular. He submits that no other independent or direct evidence has corroborated on the point that due to the gun shot fired by the appellants the victim died. He lastly submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in affirming the judgment of the trial Court in respect of the present appellants on the basis of contradictory findings while on the same footing other accused persons have been acquitted by the High Court Division. As such the judgment and order impugned herein is liable to be set aside. 

 9. Mr. Khondker Diliruzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing for the state, submits that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment as the materials on record clearly proved that there are corroborative evidence in support of the prosecution case regarding the appellants' overt act in commission of the offence. Moreover, circumstantial evidence has also proved their involvement in causing death to the victim. So the appeal should be dismissed. 

 'when a witness is declared hostile his evidence may not be rejected as a whole but which has not been discredited may be accepted if corroborated by other witnesses in material particulars'. 

 12. Under such circumstance PWs 7,10 and 11 remain as only witnesses whose evidence is very much essential to dispose of this appeal. 

 13. Out of these three witnesses PW 7 and 10 is the same person, Hamida Banu, wife of the deceased, who admittedly did not see the occurrence as she in her evidence stated that 'she was at home and heard the sound of gunshot and then came to the place of occurrence upon hearing hue and cry and found her husband dying. She does not know who killed him.' So only witness remains is PW-11, upon whom the entire responsibility falls to prove the prosecution case beyond reasonable doubt. Let us see what P.W.11 has stated in his evidence. PW-11 deposed as follows: 

 19. Comparing the above evidence of the aforesaid three hostile witnesses with those of PW-11 we do not find any corroboration on any material particular for involving or implicating the present appellants in firing the gun shots which resulted in death of the victim. PW-11 in his very short evidence stated “আমি শুনিয়াছি যে, আসামীগণ পরষ্পর একযোগে হাতেম আলীকে গুলি করিয়া খুন করিয়াছে, আমি খুনের ঘটনা দেখি নাই” this particular assertion cannot, in any way, be treated as corroboration of the allegation that the victim died as a result of the gun-shot fired by the present appellants. Rather there is nothing in the evidence of PW-11 which could corroborate any of the statements of the hostile witnesses. 

 20. In the impugned judgment it appears that the High Court Division relied on PWs-3 and 4 who also made statements under section 164 of the Code before the Magistrate and relying on such 164 statements comparing with the evidence adduced by the PWs-3 and 4 it came to a conclusion that "PW-3 and 4 are eye witnesses to the occurrence and they under aforesaid circumstances deliberately and consciously concealed the truth and thus both were declared hostile." In passing the impugned judgment the High Court Division took into consideration the demeanor of the witnesses and held "it can easily be presumed what prevented them from telling the truth. It appears that they appeared before the Court passing over the reign of terror. The wife of the deceased herself was put before the Court but prosecution compelled to tender her since she kept her mouth locked. It is true that she was not the eye-witness to the occurrence but she faced the tragic loss of her two sons earlier, her husband, (deceased) and another son, the informant to this case. From the attending circumstances of the case, we don't find it difficult to guess the atmosphere under which they became shrink from making their heart free." It is to be noted that such finding of the High Court Division is completely on guess or surmise which can never be the basis of holding a person guilty. 

 21. In criminal justice system it is well settled that a statement made under section 164 of the code by a witness is never a substantive piece of evidence. It may be used only for corroborating or contradicting a witness with his evidence in the Court. 

 22. In the present case it is required to see how far the statement of PWs 3 and 4 made under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code are acceptable in evidence to hold the accused guilty as charged. Under section 164, the Magistrate is empowered to record any statement given by a witness or confession made by an accused person to him in course of an investigation under Chapter XIV of the Code or any time afterwards before the commencement of the inquiry or trial. So it appears that two types of per-sons can be produced before the Magistrate for recording statement or confession. First one is a witness and second one is an accused, whose statement or confession may be recorded by the Magistrate if the same is voluntary. A statement made under section 164 of the Code cannot be used as substantive evidence; it can only be used in cross examining the maker thereof only to show that it was false. In the case of Abu Taher Chowdhury and others Vs. State, reported in 42 DLR(AD)252 this Division held: 

 "the statement of an witness made under section 164 Cr.P.C is meant for binding him down to the statement made during investigation. The defence may use it to contradict the witness, whereas the prosecution may use it to corroborate him when he gives evidence in court." 

 23. For the purpose of disposal of this appeal, we are concerned only with one part of section 164, which deals with recording of statement of a witness. In this case PWs 3 and 4 gave their statements before the Magistrate under section 164 of the Code. But both of them deviated from the statements already made before the Magistrate when they deposed in Court and as such they were declared hostile. Under such circumstances their evidence may not be rejected as a whole but the portion which has not been discredited may be accepted, of course if corroborated by other witnesses in material particulars, as decided in the case of Aminul Islam Bulbul Vs. State (21 BLC(AD)232). 

 24. On the other hand a statement of a witness under section 164 of the Code can never be the only basis of convicting an accused firstly, because such statement cannot be used against any accused person other than to contradict the maker of it as the same is neither a sworn statement nor open to cross-examination. Thus no reliance can be placed upon such statement recorded under section 164 of the Code. In every case the main question before a court of law is to discover the truth from the conflicting pleas of the parties before it. The requirement is not that the witness must be suppressing the truth or not desirous of telling the truth. It is the duty of the court to weigh the veracity of the evidence'. When a witness resiles at the trial from his statement made under section 164 he is declared hostile and may be cross examined by the party who produced him as witness. 

 25. In the case of Siddique Munshi Vs. State (12 BLD(AD)59) this Division has spelt out as to how the credibility of the evidence of a witness who has been declared hostile is to be dealt with. In the said case it has been held: 

 "A witness is not necessarily hostile if he reveals the truth. Established practice, now forming a rule of law, regarding the evidence of a hostile witness is that the whole of his evidence so far as it affects both the parties, favourably or unfavourably, must be considered and the court which gets the opportunity to observe his demeanour is at liberty to make assessment of the evidence. If corroboration from other source is available, of the evidence of a hostile witness, there is no reason why his evidence should be rejected outright. If the evidence of a hostile witness fits in with the attending circumstances, then it may be accepted and considered along with other evidence." 

 26. In the case in hand, the evidence of PWs 3 and 4 have already been discussed earlier. 

 27. From their evidence of PWs 3 and 4 it has already been found that both of them stated that 'they do not know how the deceased Hatem Ali died nor they know anything about the case. While they were cross examined by the prosecution, PW 3 specifically denied the suggestion that on the date of occurrence, 06.09.1999 at around 9.00 PM he along with the deceased and others while going home were surrounded by the accused persons and 18/19 others and accused Sayed asked the deceased as to why the Shahijahan's criminal case is not being withdrawn, at that stage accused bony fired his gun targeting the deceased Hatem Ali, which hit at his back and accused Humayan again fired from his gun as a result he fell down on the ground or the accused persons threatened everyone with dire consequences if any one says anything regarding the occurrence. In his cross examination he said “হাতেম কিভাবে মারা গিয়াছে আমি জানি না।” 

 29. It has also been discussed earlier that among the rest of the independent witnesses, namely PWs 7, 10, 11 and 12, PW 7 and 10 is the same person, who is the wife of the deceased. As PW 7 she was tendered and she said nothing but as PW 10 she deposed and gave her statements and she was cross examined wherein he stated that আগে সাক্ষী দিতে আসিয়া ছিলাম। আমাকে টেন্ডার করা হয়। Admittedly she is not an eye witness. PW-12 was also declared hostile when he in his evidence said 'he does not know how Hatem Ali died. He does not know anything about the occurrence. In cross examination he denied all the suggestions of the prosecution. But he did not make any statement under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Thus PW 11 remains to be the only witness, who according to the prosecution, is the eye witnesses of the occurrence. It has been found from his evidence that he did not corroborate PWs 3, 4, 7 or 10 or 12. As such the statements given by PWs 3 and 4 under section 164 of the Code having not been corroborated by either of the witnesses rather they having deviated from their own statements made under section 164 were declared hostile and their evidence/statements cannot be relied upon. Nor any other witness corroborated them or any corroboration from other sources is available to accept their evidence which fits in to accept or consider their evidence along with other evidence. Thus on analysing their evidence, nothing is found from which it can be construed that the accused appellants are the assailants of the deceased Hatem Ali and they killed the victim. 

 30. In the present case the makers of such statements were produced as PWs. 3 and 4, who in their evidence clearly denied that they made any statement before the Magistrate. They said Babor Ali took them to the Police Station and then to the Court and took their thumb impression. PW3 specifically said Babor Ali threatened him and obtained thumb impression otherwise he would be implicated in murder case. Neither Babor Ali read over the same to him nor he read the contents written in the paper. He does not know how Hatem died. Similar was the version of PW-4. He also said that he did not make any statement before the magistrate. He was taken to the Court where his thumb impression was obtained. So it is clear that the makers of the 164 statements totally denied making such statements and as such the contents of the same cannot be considered for convicting the accused persons. 

 32. The High Court Division considered the inquest and the post mortem reports, and observed that 'Both inquest and autopsy report support the allegation that accused Johny and Humayun Kabir fired the gun shots on the deceased.' The High Court Division taking into consideration the seized blood stained earth(mud) and fired cartridge/bullet also held that the same 'provide corroboration to the occurrence of causing death to the deceased by fire arm at the place of occurrence wherefrom the materials were seized immediately after the occurrence at 11.00 p.m.' and accordingly came to a conclusion "It appears from the evidence on record that the accused Johny and Humayun Kabir caused death to the deceased by gun fire". Basing on such observation and findings the High Court Division concluded saying "we find no hesitation to come to this view that prosecution aptly proved the guilt against the convict appellants Johny and Humayun Kabir who committed death to the deceased by gunshot...." 

 33. This finding of the High Court Division is totally erroneous because there is no direct or independent evidence on record from any of the eye witnesses, as discussed earlier, that the victim died because of the gun shots fired by the appellants. The High Court Division took an erroneous view basing on the allegations made in the FIR which, according to the High Court Division, is corroborated by the inquest report, seized alamats and autopsy report. The allegation made in the FIR is not an evidence. It may be used for the purpose of corroboration or contradiction of the maker. For the purpose of proving the allegations made in the FIR the prosecution is required to prove the same both by oral and documentary evidence beyond reasonable doubt. The documentary evidence like inquest report or the post mortem report cannot in every case prove as to who committed the offence. It can at best prove commission of some offence. But who committed the offence is a question of fact to be proved by adducing oral evidence either direct or circumstantial. Here in this case, as has been discussed earlier, none of the PWs could prove either by direct evidence or there is any circumstantial evidence which proved, beyond reasonable doubt, that the victim died as a result of gunshots fired by the appellants. A conviction cannot be given on surmises or conjecture/guess. The Court is to find from the evidence on record that the prosecution has been able to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that it is the accused who has committed the offence. In the present case the documentary evidence might have proved the death of the victim by gunshot. But those documents can never prove who fired the gun-shot. The prosecution produced 3(three) alleged eye witnesses, who, were declared hostile, and miserably failed to prove that the appellants were the assailants. 

 34. By now it has already been settled in criminal justice system that a statement of a witness under section 164 cannot be taken as substantive evidence because the said statement has been recorded in the absence of the accused and the accused has not cross-examined him at the time of making such statement. The credibility of such witness, becomes more discredited if he goes away from his earlier statement or makes inconsistent statement, when produced and examined as a P.W, unless his evidence is corroborated in material particulars by other PWs. When a prosecution witness is declared hostile, the court under such circumstances, in its discretion may allow the party, who calls him as witness, to put any question in the form of cross-examination. Such discretion is unqualified and is quite apart from any question to the hostility. The value of the evidence of such hostile witness, cross examined by the party calling him, cannot he used for or against either party. Such witness loses all evidentiary value. When a witness has been discredited on one point he may not be given credit on another. Before relying upon the evidence of such witness it is to be considered that previously he made an unsworn statement before the Magistrate, which cannot be used as an evidence against the accused. The evidence of such witness must be received with caution. If there is no other evidence to corroborate the evidence of such hostile witness it cannot be taken into consideration against the accused. As a matter of prudence, on the facts of the case, it would be hazardous to allow the prosecution to take advantage of the evidence of such witnesses. When these witnesses contradicted substantially with their previous statements and as a result of the cross-examination, their credit was substantially, if not wholly, shaken. It was therefore, not proper for the court to pick up a few sentences from the evidence/statements and use the same for the purpose of convicting, the accused persons. The above view finds support in the case of Sat Paul Vs. Delhi Administration (1976, 1 SCC 727). In the present case the High Court Division fell in error in maintaining the conviction of the appellants relying on the uncorroborated evidence of the hostile PWS.3, 4 and 12 in the offence of killing the victim Hatem Ali. 

 35. In the light of the 12 BLD Case, this Court, upon assessing the evidence of PWs. 3, 4 and 12 along with other witnesses did not find any corroboration from other available source to accept the evidence of the hostile witnesses which could fit in with the attending circumstances to consider the same. Thus it can easily be held that under no circumstances the prosecution has been able to prove that the charges brought against the present appellants have been proved beyond reasonable doubt, basing upon which they could be convicted. 

 36. Accordingly we hold that the High Court Division came to an erroneous finding relying on the evidence of such witnesses, which are unconfirmed and uncorroborated by any other independent evidence, and thereby came to an erroneous finding in holding that the appellants were the assailants and by their gunshots the victim died. It is highly unsafe to convict the appellants on the basis of such uncorroborated testimony of PWs. 3,4 and 12. 

 37. The prosecution having totally failed to prove the case against the appellants beyond reasonable doubt the Courts below erred in law in relying upon such unfounded and uncorroborated evidence and also on the testimony of the hostile witnesses as well as upon the other evidence, uncorroborated on material particulars, which are beyond the principle of criminal justice system. As such the decision convicting and sentencing the appellants on such unfounded evidence is not sustainable in law. Hence we find merit in this appeal.
